## Questions and answers
### What is a B-lender?
A federally or provincially regulated lender — like a trust company or credit union — that takes on files banks decline. Rates are higher, but the path to ownership is real.

### How are B-lender rates different?
Typically 1–3% higher than A-lender rates, plus a lender fee. I'm transparent about this upfront — there are no surprises on closing day.

### Will applying hurt my credit score?
A single mortgage application is one hard inquiry — minimal impact. I do a soft pull first before we go anywhere near a formal application.

### How long until I can refinance to A-lender rates?
Usually 12–24 months of on-time payments and a recovering credit profile is enough. I track this with you and tell you when you're ready.

### What documents do I need?
Depends on your situation — but typically ID, 3–6 months of bank statements, proof of income (T4, NOA, or business financials), and a property address. I'll give you a specific list on our first call.

### What are your fees?
I'm paid by the lender on most deals. On some private/B files there's a brokerage fee — I'll tell you the exact number before you commit to anything.

### What is a private mortgage?
A short-term loan, usually one to two years, from a private lender or mortgage investment company. It's approved mainly on your property's equity rather than your income or credit. It costs more than a B-lender, so I use it as a bridge: solve the problem now, then move you to a better rate.

## Mortgages for buying a home
A first mortgage is the main loan on the home you buy. I shop it across lenders, get you pre-approved, and stay on the file until you have the keys.
- How long does a pre-approval last? Most lenders hold the rate for 90 to 120 days. If you have not bought by then, we renew it at whatever rate applies at the time.
- Is a pre-approval a guarantee? No. The lender still has to approve the property itself and confirm your documents. It does tell you what you can realistically spend.
- Fixed or variable? It depends on how much payment movement you can live with and how long you plan to keep the home. I lay out both side by side before you choose.

## Mortgages for first-time home buyers
Buying your first home comes with more programs and rules than most people expect. I'll show you which ones you qualify for and how much they can save you.
- Who counts as a first-time buyer? Definitions vary by program. Some count you as first-time if you haven't owned a home you lived in during the last four years. I check each program against your history.
- Can my parents help with the down payment? Usually, yes, as a gift. Lenders want a signed letter confirming it is a gift and not a loan, and proof the money is in your account.
- What if my credit is thin or I was declined? That's the work I specialise in. There are lenders for short credit histories and non-traditional income, and I'll tell you which fits.

## Mortgages for newcomers to Canada
Moved to Canada recently? You can buy a home before you've built years of Canadian credit. There are programs built for exactly this.
- Can I get a mortgage with no Canadian credit history? Often, yes. Some programs accept other proof of payment history, like rent or utilities, in place of a long Canadian credit file.
- Can I use money from outside Canada for my down payment? Usually, yes. Lenders will want to see where it came from and, in most cases, that it has been in a Canadian account for a while. I'll tell you exactly what your lender needs.
- Do I need to be a permanent resident? No. There are options for work-permit holders too, though the down payment is usually higher.

## Mortgages for self-employed people
Self-employed borrowers get declined because their tax returns show what's left after write-offs, not what the business really earns. I work with lenders who look at the whole picture.
- How long do I need to have been self-employed? Most lenders want about two years in business. Some will consider less if you worked in the same line of work before going out on your own.
- Do I need 20% down? For most B-lender self-employed programs, yes. Some insured programs allow less down when your income can be verified on paper. I check which applies to you.
- Can lenders use my bank statements instead of my tax return? Some can. They use your deposits to show what the business really brings in. It depends on the lender and your file, and I'll tell you on the first call which way works for you.

## Mortgage renewal
When your term ends, your lender sends a renewal offer, and many people simply sign it. It's the one time you can move without a penalty, so it's worth a second look.
- Do I have to pass the stress test to switch lenders at renewal? Usually not, if you're keeping the same amount and amortization. That rule changed in late 2024. Borrowing more at renewal is treated differently.
- Does switching lenders cost anything? Often very little: many lenders cover the legal and appraisal costs on a straight switch. I'll confirm the costs for your lender.
- Can I take out equity when I renew? Yes. That's a refinance at renewal, and it's often the cheapest time to do it because there's no penalty to break your term.

## Mortgage refinancing
Refinancing replaces your mortgage with a new one, usually to lower your payments, pay off high-interest debt, or take equity out of your home.
- How much does it cost to refinance? Expect a legal fee, usually an appraisal, and a penalty if you're mid-term. I lay out the full cost next to the savings so you can see whether it's worth it.
- Can I refinance with bad credit? Often, yes, through a B-lender or a private lender, as long as you have enough equity in your home.
- Should I refinance now or wait for my renewal? If your renewal is close, making changes at renewal avoids a penalty. If it's far off and you're carrying high-interest debt, refinancing now can still save money. It comes down to the numbers.

## Debt consolidation mortgages
Credit cards and personal loans can cost far more than a mortgage. Moving that debt onto your home can cut what you pay each month, and get you back on track.
- How much can I consolidate? Usually up to about 80% of your home value, minus what you owe on your mortgage. Private lenders may go a little higher.
- Will it improve my credit score? Paying off maxed-out cards and then paying on time usually helps over time. Closing accounts or running the cards back up can work against you.
- Should I refinance or take a second mortgage? If breaking your current mortgage costs a lot, a second mortgage may be cheaper. If not, a refinance is usually cheaper. I'll run both.

## Second mortgages
A second mortgage lets you borrow against your home without touching the mortgage you already have. You keep your current rate on the first.
- Do I need good credit for a second mortgage? Not always. Many second mortgages come from B-lenders or private lenders who focus on your equity more than your credit score.
- Is a second mortgage the same as a HELOC? Not quite. A second mortgage is usually a lump sum with set payments. A HELOC is a credit line you draw on as needed, and usually needs stronger credit.
- Can I pay it off early? Often, yes, but terms vary. Some private loans charge a fee for early payout. I'll tell you before you sign.

## Home equity line of credit (HELOC)
A HELOC is a line of credit secured by your home. You borrow what you need, when you need it, and pay interest only on what you've used.
- Who qualifies for a HELOC? HELOCs are mostly offered by banks and A-lenders, so they need good credit and provable income. If that is not you yet, a second mortgage may fit better.
- Is the rate fixed? Usually not. Most HELOCs are variable, tied to the lender’s prime rate, so the cost moves with interest rates.
- Can I add a HELOC when I renew? Often, yes. Renewal is a good time to set one up because you're already reviewing the mortgage.

## Spousal buyout mortgages
Separation is hard enough without losing the home. A spousal buyout mortgage lets one of you keep it by paying out the other's share of the equity.
- Do I need a separation agreement first? For most lenders, yes. It's what tells them the buyout amount. Talk to your lawyer, and I'll tell you what the lender will need it to say.
- Can I borrow more than 80% of the home value? With some lenders and an insured spousal buyout program, yes, up to 95% in some cases. It depends on the lender and your file.
- Can support payments count as income? Often, if they are set out in the agreement and you can show they are being paid. Lenders treat them differently, so I check before we apply.

## Reverse mortgages
A reverse mortgage lets homeowners 55 and older turn part of their home's value into tax-free cash, without monthly mortgage payments and without selling.
- Is the money taxable? No. It's a loan, not income, so it isn't taxed and generally doesn't affect Old Age Security or the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
- Do I have to make monthly payments? No. You can pay the interest if you want to, but you don't have to. The loan is repaid when the home is sold or you move out.
- Will my family still inherit the home? Your estate keeps whatever equity is left once the loan is repaid. Many families sell the home and keep the difference, or repay the loan and keep the home.

## B-lender mortgages in the GTA
A bank decline isn't the end of the road. B-lenders are regulated trust companies and credit unions that look at the files the big banks turn away, and they're where most of my clients start.
- Is a B-lender safe? Yes. B-lenders are regulated lenders, not loan sharks. Your mortgage is a normal registered mortgage with a set term and set payments. The difference is the rate and the approval rules.
- How much down payment does a B-lender need? Usually 20% for a purchase, because most B-lender mortgages are uninsured. On a refinance you can typically borrow up to about 80% of your home’s value.
- Will a B-lender mortgage stop me getting a bank mortgage later? No. Paying it on time is exactly what rebuilds your file. Most of my B-lender clients plan to move back to a bank within one or two terms.

## Private mortgages and private lending
When even a B-lender can't help in time, a private mortgage can. It's short-term money secured by your property's equity, used to fix a problem now and set up something better next.
- How long does a private mortgage last? Usually one year, sometimes two. Payments are often interest-only. The point is to give you time to fix the problem, then move to a cheaper lender.
- Can I get a private mortgage with bad credit? Often, yes, if there is enough equity in the property. Private lenders care most about the equity and the plan to repay.
- What is a private second mortgage? A loan registered behind your existing mortgage. You keep your current mortgage and its rate, and borrow against the equity on top of it.

## Commercial mortgages
Commercial lending runs on different rules from home mortgages. Lenders look at the property and its income as much as at you, and I find the ones that fit your deal.
- How much down payment do I need for a commercial property? Usually 25% to 35%, depending on the property type and lender. Some multi-unit residential programs allow less.
- How long does commercial financing take? Longer than a home mortgage: appraisals and environmental reports can add weeks. Start early, especially with a firm closing date.
- Can I get a commercial mortgage with a newer business? It's harder but possible, particularly if the property itself has strong income or you have a larger down payment.

## Agriculture and farm lending
Farms and rural property need lenders who understand them. Many banks treat acreage as unusual, but there are lenders who specialise in it.
- Is a hobby farm treated like a working farm? Usually not. A hobby farm is generally financed like a rural home, with limits on how much land counts. A working farm is assessed as a business.
- Can I use farm income to qualify? Yes, with lenders that understand agriculture. They'll want a few years of farm financial statements.
- Do you handle rural properties outside the GTA? Yes, across Ontario. Rural lending is about finding the right lender for the property, and I'll tell you up front if one is a hard fit.
